label: The Gluing Machine
notes: This chapter turns the fundamental group from a one-space-at-a-time invariant into a gluing machine. When a path-connected space is built from two open pieces with path-connected overlap, its fundamental group is assembled from the piece groups plus exactly the identifications forced by overlap loops.

label: Statement of the Theorem
notes: State the hypotheses carefully: U, V, and their intersection must all be open and path-connected, with the base point in the overlap. Under these conditions the fundamental group of the union is the pushout, a free product amalgamated over the intersection group.

label: The Pushout of Groups
notes: The induced inclusions give a commuting square of group homomorphisms. The fundamental group of X is the universal object completing that square: the free product of the two piece groups quotiented by the normal closure of all words comparing the two images of each overlap loop.

label: Why Surjectivity Holds
notes: Any loop in X is subdivided by a Lebesgue number so each short arc lands in U or in V. Connector paths to the base point convert each arc into a based loop in one piece, so alternating letters from the two piece groups generate the whole fundamental group.

label: The Normal Closure Ledger
notes: A loop living in the overlap has two names: one through U, one through V. These are different free-product letters but the same loop in X. The theorem says this is the only ambiguity, so we quotient by the normal closure of every comparison word.

label: The Proof-Square Sweep
notes: For the kernel, take a null-homotopy of a trivial word and subdivide its square so each small cell maps into U or V. Sweep the bottom word upward row by row to the constant top edge; each crossing contributes exactly one overlap relation already in the normal closure.

label: Two Special Cases
notes: Two reductions do most of the work. If the overlap is simply connected, the union group is just the free product. If one piece is simply connected, it adds no generators but its overlap loops can still impose relations, turning the other piece group into a quotient.

label: Wedges and the Free Group
notes: For a wedge of circles, thicken each summand using the nondegenerate base point so the overlap becomes contractible. The simply connected intersection case then gives a free product, so the figure-eight has fundamental group the free group on two generators, and n circles give the free group of rank n.

label: Graphs and Spanning Trees
notes: Every finite connected graph has a contractible spanning tree contributing nothing. The edges outside the tree are the loops that cannot collapse. With V vertices and E edges there are E minus V plus one chords, and that cycle rank equals the rank of the free fundamental group.

label: Spheres are Simply Connected
notes: Cover the n-sphere by two open caps overlapping in an equatorial band homotopy equivalent to a smaller sphere. For n at least two that band is path-connected and both caps are contractible, so the simply connected overlap case forces the fundamental group of the sphere to be trivial.

label: CW Complexes as Presentations
notes: A finite CW complex computes its fundamental group in layers. The one-skeleton gives free generators after choosing a spanning tree, each attached two-cell adds its boundary word as a relator, and cells of dimension at least three leave the group unchanged because their punctured overlap is simply connected.

label: Compact Surface Groups
notes: A surface polygon word becomes a group presentation: edges are generators, the single face is the relator. Orientable genus g gives a product of commutators with abelianization the integers to the 2g; nonorientable genus n gives a product of squares with abelianization carrying one order-two factor.

label: Recap and Takeaways
notes: The theorem is a controlled recipe: the free product records loops in either set, overlap relations identify the two names of a shared loop. Graphs give free groups, two-cells add relators, and surface polygon words yield the standard presentations whose abelianizations separate the compact surface families.
